claim: fMRI patterns of voxel activity in human early visual cortex can be used to decode the contents of visual working memory
source: Following now classic studies demonstrating that fMRI patterns of voxel activity in human early visual cortex can be used to decode the contents of visual working memory (WM; Harrison and Tong, 2009; Serences et al., 2009)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Harrison and Tong, 2009 and Serences et al., 2009

claim: The sensory recruitment hypothesis posits that visual WM storage utilizes the encoding machinery in the visual cortex
source: This incredibly influential hypothesis posits that visual WM storage utilizes the encoding machinery in the visual cortex, assuming that memory and perception utilize similar mechanisms (Postle, 2006; Curtis and D'Esposito, 2003; D'Esposito and Postle, 2015; Serences, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple sources describing the sensory recruitment hypothesis

claim: WM representations can be decoded from the activity patterns as early as primary visual cortex (V1)
source: On the one hand, WM representations can be decoded from the activity patterns as early as primary visual cortex (V1; Harrison and Tong, 2009; Serences et al., 2009; Riggall and Postle, 2012; Sprague et al., 2014; Rahmati et al., 2018; Curtis and Sprague, 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to studies demonstrating WM decoding from V1

claim: Classifiers trained on data collected from early visual cortex while participants are viewing stimuli can be used to decode the contents of WM
source: There is even some evidence that classifiers trained on data collected from early visual cortex while participants are simply viewing stimuli (e.g. oriented gratings) can be used to decode the contents of WM (Harrison and Tong, 2009; Rademaker et al., 2019; Albers et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies showing cross-decoding between perception and WM

claim: If sensory representations generated via bottom-up processing are interchangeable with WM representations, then the representation itself is perceptual in nature
source: The assumption here is that if sensory representations generated via bottom-up processing are interchangeable with WM representations, then the representation itself is perceptual in nature (although see Lee et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a theoretical assumption stated in the text with a citation to Lee et al., 2012 for a contrasting view

claim: The neural circuitry in early visual cortex can simultaneously maintain WM representations while encoding incoming and potentially distracting percepts
source: Some evidence suggests, however, that the neural circuitry in early visual cortex can simultaneously maintain WM representations while encoding incoming and potentially distracting percepts (Hallenbeck et al., 2021; Rademaker et al., 2019; Lorenc et al., 2018; Iamshchinina et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: Trialwise variations in decoded WM representations predict key behavioral factors like errors and uncertainty of memory
source: Moreover, trialwise variations in these decoded WM representations predict key behavioral factors like errors (Ester et al., 2013) and uncertainty of memory (Li et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies showing behavioral correlations

claim: Distractor-induced distortions in WM representations predict the direction and degree of distractor-induced memory errors
source: Distractor-induced distortions in WM representations also predict the direction and degree of distractor-induced memory errors (Hallenbeck et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hallenbeck et al., 2021

claim: Memory-guided behaviors depend on a readout of WM representations in early visual cortex
source: Together, it appears as if memory-guided behaviors depend on a readout of these representations in early visual cortex.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the preceding evidence about behavioral correlations

claim: Persistent activity is not characteristic of V1 neurons, with perhaps the exception of spatial WM
source: With perhaps the exception of spatial WM (Saber et al., 2015; Hallenbeck et al., 2021; Li and Curtis, 2023; van Kerkoerle et al., 2017; Supèr et al., 2001), persistent activity, the most conclusive neural mechanism of WM, is not characteristic of V1 neurons (Leavitt et al., 2017; Curtis and Sprague, 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: Decoding WM content from perception-trained classifiers is usually worse compared to when WM data are used to train decoders
source: However, decoding is usually worse compared to when WM data are used to train decoders (Harrison and Tong, 2009; Rademaker et al., 2019), especially in parietal cortex (Albers et al., 2013; Rademaker et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies comparing decoding performance

claim: WM representations in early visual cortex appear to change over time from encoding to maintenance throughout the retention interval
source: WM representations in early visual cortex also appear to change over time from when encoding the memoranda to its maintenance throughout the retention interval.
evidence: This is stated as a general finding in the literature

claim: Changes in WM representations appear to reflect reformatting from one that is more sensory-like to one that is more connected to the demands of the memory-guided behavior
source: These changes appear to reflect reformatting of the representation from one that is more sensory-like to one during WM that is more connected to the demands of the memory-guided behavior (Kwak and Curtis, 2022; Li and Curtis, 2023; Henderson et al., 2022)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies showing reformatting

claim: Reformatting of WM representations may explain how WM representations in V1 survive distraction
source: and may explain how WM representations in V1 survive distraction (Rademaker et al., 2019; Hallenbeck et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation supported by citations

claim: Successful orientation decoding depends on the unique patterns of activity originating from inhomogeneous sampling of orientation columns at fine scales across voxels
source: The general linking hypothesis, therefore, assumes that successful orientation decoding depends on the unique patterns of activity originating from inhomogeneous sampling of orientation columns at fine scales across voxels (Boynton, 2005; Haynes and Rees, 2005; Kamitani and Tong, 2005).
evidence: The claim describes a hypothesis supported by citations

claim: Coarse, not fine, scale biases at the retinotopic map level underlie decoding of orientation during perception
source: However, recent research suggests that coarse, not fine, scale biases at the retinotopic map level, such as a global preference for cardinal and radial orientations (Freeman et al., 2011; Freeman et al., 2013; Mannion et al., 2010; Roth et al., 2022) underlie decoding of orientation during perception.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to recent research

claim: Orientation decoding relies on complex interactions between the stimulus's orientation, its bounding aperture, and topographic inhomogeneities across the visual field map
source: Rather than just a reflection of fine-scale sampling of orientation tuned neurons, orientation decoding also relies on complex interactions between the stimulus's orientation, its bounding aperture, and topographic inhomogeneities across the visual field map (Carlson, 2014; Roth et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to theoretical and empirical work

claim: It remains unknown how WM decoding might be affected by coarse-scale biases
source: Despite changes to the hypothesis linking successful decoding of perceived orientation to its underlying causes, it remains unknown how WM decoding might be affected by these coarse-scale biases.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge that motivates the current study

claim: The radial modulator evokes a coarse-scale bias aligned with the carrier orientation
source: Specifically, the radial modulator evokes a coarse-scale bias aligned with the carrier orientation, while the angular modulator evokes a coarse-scale bias orthogonal to the carrier orientation (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1C showing the model predictions

claim: The angular modulator evokes a coarse-scale bias orthogonal to the carrier orientation
source: Specifically, the radial modulator evokes a coarse-scale bias aligned with the carrier orientation, while the angular modulator evokes a coarse-scale bias orthogonal to the carrier orientation (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1C showing the model predictions

claim: If the format of the memorized orientation is sensory-like in nature, decoding would conform with the aperture bias
source: We predicted that if the format of the memorized orientation is sensory-like in nature, decoding would conform with the aperture bias.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the sensory recruitment hypothesis

claim: During perception, classifiers trained to decode the orientation of gratings altered by one type of modulator could only decode the orientation of gratings altered by the same type of modulator
source: As predicted, we replicated (Roth et al., 2018) that classifiers trained to decode the orientation of gratings altered by one type of modulator could only decode the orientation of gratings altered by the same type of modulator (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1; within).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2A and replicates prior work

claim: During perception, classifiers could not cross-decode orientation gratings altered by the other type of modulator
source: Classifiers could not cross-decode orientation gratings altered by the other type of modulator (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1; cross) presumably because classification depends on aperture biases that are orthogonal for radial and angular modulated gratings.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2A with an inference about the mechanism

claim: Aperture bias effects during perception were limited to visual field maps in early visual cortex (V1-V3)
source: Note that these effects were limited to visual field maps in early visual cortex (V1-V3).
evidence: This is an observation from the data analysis

claim: Orientations could be decoded during the WM late delay epoch in visual and parietal cortex separately for each type of modulator
source: We first validated our methods by replicating successful orientation decoding in visual and parietal cortex separately for each type of modulator (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 2; within; Emrich et al., 2013; Ester et al., 2015; Harrison and Tong, 2009; Kwak and Curtis, 2022; Riggall and Postle, 2012; Sarma et al., 2016; Serences et al., 2009; Yu and Shim, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2B and replicates prior studies

claim: During WM maintenance, classifiers trained on oriented gratings with one type of modulator could successfully cross-decode gratings with the other type of modulator
source: Indeed, we found that despite the orthogonal aperture biases induced by the two modulators, their patterns during WM maintenance were interchangeable. Within visual field maps in early and mid visual cortex (V1, V2, V3, V3AB), parietal cortex (IPS0/1, IPS2/3), and frontal cortex (sPCS), classifiers trained on different modulators could cross-decode the orientation of gratings (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 2; cross).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2B

claim: WM representations of orientation are immune to the aperture biases demonstrated during perception
source: These results indicate that WM representations of orientation are immune to the aperture biases we demonstrated during perception.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the cross-decoding results

claim: In early visual cortex (V1-V3), classifiers trained during perception can be used to decode orientation information in WM, but only when the aperture bias is aligned with the orientation of the grating
source: In early visual cortex (V1-V3), we found that classifiers trained during perception can be used to decode orientation information in WM, but only when the aperture bias is aligned with the orientation of the grating (i.e. radial modulator; Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 3; within).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2C

claim: In early visual cortex, significant WM decoding across modulator types was only observed when classifiers were trained during perception of the radial but not angular modulated grating
source: Similarly, we only observed significant WM decoding across modulator types in early visual cortex when classifiers were trained during perception of the radial (aligned with orientation) but not angular (orthogonal to orientation) modulated grating (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 3; cross).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2C

claim: WM representations of orientation are only similar to perceptual representations when they happen to align with the aperture biases induced during perception
source: These results indicate that WM representations of orientation, which are not biased by aperture, are only similar to perceptual representations when they happen to align with the aperture biases induced during perception.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the cross-task decoding results

claim: V3AB was a notable exception in that orientation could be decoded regardless of the type of modulator used for training or testing
source: Note that V3AB was a notable exception in that orientation could be decoded regardless of the type of modulator used for training or testing.
evidence: This is an observation from the data analysis

claim: WM representations in early visual cortex are distinct from perceptual representations
source: The results thus far imply that WM representations in early visual cortex are distinct from perceptual representations.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the preceding results

claim: WM representations are immune to the aperture biases during perception because they have been recoded into another format during memory
source: Moreover, WM representations are immune to the aperture biases during perception perhaps because they have been recoded into another format during memory.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed results

claim: Participants recoded in WM the carrier orientation of gratings into line-like images encoded in the spatial distribution of response amplitudes across topographic maps
source: We hypothesized that participants recoded in WM the carrier orientation of gratings, regardless of the type of modulator, into line-like images encoded in the spatial distribution of response amplitudes across topographic maps (Kwak and Curtis, 2022; Li et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citations to prior work

claim: Line-like representations emerged during the WM delay in V1-V3AB and IPS0/1
source: Clearly, the visualization technique confirmed our hypothesis and revealed a line encoded in the amplitudes of voxel activity at the angle matching the target orientation during the WM delay in V1-V3AB and IPS0/1 (Figure 3A), but not other ROIs (see Figure 3—figure supplement 1 for details).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A

claim: Line-like representations during WM were matched to the carrier orientation and not the aperture biases induced by the modulator
source: Critically, these line-like representations were matched to the carrier orientation and not the aperture biases induced by the modulator.
evidence: This is an observation from the spatial reconstruction analysis

claim: During the perception task, the angle of the line-like patterns depended on the type of modulator in early visual areas (V1 and V2)
source: Unlike the WM task, during the perception task the angle of the line-like patterns depended on the type of modulator in early visual areas (V1 and V2), where the line matched the orientation of the aperture bias, not the carrier.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3C

claim: During perception, the line is orthogonal to the angular modulated carrier in early visual cortex (V1 and V2) but not in later visual field maps
source: Note how the line is orthogonal to the angular modulated carrier in early visual cortex (V1 and V2) but not in later visual field maps (e.g. V3A/B).
evidence: This is an observation from Figure 3C

claim: During the perception task, line-like representations in early visual cortex for radial but not angular modulated orientations result in strong filtered responses and fidelities
source: During the perception task, the line-like representations in early visual cortex for radial but not angular modulated orientations result in strong filtered responses and fidelities.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3D

claim: The spatial maps based on model responses matched those in the perception control task
source: The spatial maps based on model responses matched those in the perception control task.
evidence: This is a comparison between model simulations and empirical data

claim: Model spatial maps showed a clear orthogonal orientation bias induced by the stimulus aperture
source: They showed a clear orthogonal orientation bias induced by the stimulus aperture, while the results for line-like images matched the spatial profile of neural activity during the WM delay.
evidence: This is an observation from the model simulations

claim: Results for line-like images matched the spatial profile of neural activity during the WM delay
source: They showed a clear orthogonal orientation bias induced by the stimulus aperture, while the results for line-like images matched the spatial profile of neural activity during the WM delay.
evidence: This is a comparison between model simulations and empirical data

claim: Mnemonic representations are flexibly recoded into a spatial topographic format that is line-like in nature with angles matching the target orientation
source: Overall, these results provide solid evidence that mnemonic representations are flexibly recoded into a spatial topographic format that is line-like in nature with angles matching the target orientation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the spatial reconstruction results

claim: WM appears immune to the aperture biases because its format is an abstraction of the perceptual features underlying the biases
source: WM appears immune to the aperture biases because its format is an abstraction of the perceptual features underlying the biases.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the overall results

claim: Neural representations of percepts are not the same as neural representations of memory, even in early visual cortex
source: As we detail next, they provide conclusive evidence that neural representations of percepts are not the same as neural representations of memory, even in early visual cortex.
evidence: This is a major conclusion of the study

claim: WM representations are reformatted abstractions of percepts
source: Instead, our evidence indicates that WM representations are reformatted abstractions of percepts.
evidence: This is a major conclusion of the study

claim: Orientation decoding was initially thought to reflect random voxel sampling of the fine-scale columnar distributions of neurons with orientation tuning
source: Initially, orientation decoding was thought to reflect random voxel sampling of the fine-scale columnar distributions of neurons with orientation tuning (Boynton, 2005; Haynes and Rees, 2005; Kamitani and Tong, 2005).
evidence: This describes a historical hypothesis supported by citations

claim: Theoretical and empirical work argued that orientation decoding depends on coarse-scale factors
source: Theoretical (Carlson, 2014) and empirical work (Freeman et al., 2011; Freeman et al., 2013; Roth et al., 2018) argued that decoding depended instead on coarse-scale factors.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to theoretical and empirical work

claim: Orientation decoding relies on the complex interaction between a grating's orientation, its bounding aperture, and the non-isotropic distribution of orientation tuned neurons across the topographic map of V1
source: Specifically, it appears that orientation decoding relies to some degree on the complex interaction between a grating's orientation, its bounding aperture, and the non-isotropic distribution of orientation tuned neurons across the topographic map of V1.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the literature

claim: fMRI decoding of orientation depends on the coarse-scale aperture biases the modulators evoke
source: (Roth et al., 2018), using the same modulated orientation gratings we used, demonstrated that fMRI decoding of orientation depends on the coarse-scale aperture biases the modulators evoke.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Roth et al., 2018

claim: The patterns of neural activity during perception of an oriented grating are distinct from the patterns during WM for the same grating
source: Together, these results provide strong and direct evidence that the patterns of neural activity during perception of an oriented grating are distinct from the patterns during WM for the same grating.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined results

claim: Line-like patterns during perception were aligned to the aperture bias rather than the grating's orientation
source: During the perception control task, the line-like patterns were also present in the population response, but the angles of these lines matched the axis of the aperture bias rather than the grating's orientation (Figure 3B), again confirming differences between perception and memory.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3B (likely referring to 3C based on context)

claim: A computational model of V1 simulated the aperture biases induced by the modulators
source: Finally, we used a computational model of V1 that simulated the aperture biases induced by the modulators (Roth et al., 2018; Simoncelli et al., 1992).
evidence: The claim describes the use of a model supported by citations

claim: Model simulations found line-like stripes across retinotopic V1 aligned to the aperture bias and not the carrier orientation
source: Consistent with our empirical data, we found line-like stripes across retinotopic V1 aligned to the aperture bias and not the carrier orientation, providing a plausible explanation for why WM decoding depends on factors other than orientation.
evidence: The claim is supported by model simulations

claim: WM for oriented gratings are reformatted into simple spatial codes, like a line
source: Instead, we propose that WM for oriented gratings, no matter what the aperture is, are reformatted into simple spatial codes, like a line (Kwak and Curtis, 2022; Li and Curtis, 2023).
evidence: This is a proposal supported by citations to prior work

claim: Line-like patterns during WM are remarkably similar to simulations of a physical line input to the model of V1
source: These line-like patterns are remarkably similar to simulations of a physical line input to the model of V1 (Figure 4), suggesting people are storing a simplified abstraction of the physical stimulus.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison with model simulations shown in Figure 4

claim: People are storing a simplified abstraction of the physical stimulus during WM
source: These line-like patterns are remarkably similar to simulations of a physical line input to the model of V1 (Figure 4), suggesting people are storing a simplified abstraction of the physical stimulus.
evidence: This is an inference from the similarity between data and model simulations

claim: WM representations do not appear to undergo normalization like perceptual representations
source: These results also may explain why WM representations do not appear to undergo normalization like perceptual representations (Bloem et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation supported by a citation

claim: WM decoding of orientation is immune to the aperture biases that drive decoding during perceptual studies of orientation
source: In summary, we found the WM decoding of orientation is immune to the aperture biases that drive decoding during perceptual studies of orientation.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding

claim: WM representations are reformatted into efficient abstractions of percepts such that they most closely support memory guided behavior
source: Moreover, WM representations are reformatted into efficient abstractions of percepts such that they most closely support memory guided behavior.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the results

claim: Oriented gratings were recoded into line-like representations during WM
source: Although our previous study also found evidence that oriented gratings were recoded into line-like representations (Kwak and Curtis, 2022), here we demonstrate that those representations are not driven by aperture biases, but instead reflect abstract line-like representations.
evidence: The claim references a prior study and extends its findings

claim: Line-like representations during WM are not driven by aperture biases, but instead reflect abstract line-like representations
source: Although our previous study also found evidence that oriented gratings were recoded into line-like representations (Kwak and Curtis, 2022), here we demonstrate that those representations are not driven by aperture biases, but instead reflect abstract line-like representations.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the current study that extends prior work

claim: These results necessitate revisions to the sensory recruitment hypothesis of WM
source: These results together necessitate revisions to the sensory recruitment hypothesis of WM because the same stimulus is supported by distinct, and not as predicted interchangeable, patterns of neural activity during perception and memory.
evidence: This is a theoretical implication drawn from the results

claim: The same stimulus is supported by distinct, and not interchangeable, patterns of neural activity during perception and memory
source: These results together necessitate revisions to the sensory recruitment hypothesis of WM because the same stimulus is supported by distinct, and not as predicted interchangeable, patterns of neural activity during perception and memory.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the data

claim: If seeing and remembering a stimulus depends on the same encoding mechanisms then one would predict an interchangeable pattern
source: If seeing and remembering a stimulus depends on the same encoding mechanisms then one would predict an interchangeable pattern.
evidence: This is a logical prediction from the sensory recruitment hypothesis

claim: The sensory recruitment hypothesis must be modified to take into account how WM representations differ from perceptual representations
source: At the very least, the sensory recruitment hypothesis must be modified to take into account both how WM representations differ from perceptual representations, and how WM representations can morph into different formats that likely depend on the goal of the memory-guided behavior.
evidence: This is a theoretical implication of the findings

claim: WM representations can morph into different formats that likely depend on the goal of the memory-guided behavior
source: At the very least, the sensory recruitment hypothesis must be modified to take into account both how WM representations differ from perceptual representations, and how WM representations can morph into different formats that likely depend on the goal of the memory-guided behavior.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the findings

claim: Sixteen neurologically healthy volunteers participated in this study
source: Sixteen neurologically healthy volunteers (including the two authors; five females; 20–54 years old) with normal or corrected-to-normal vision participated in this study.
evidence: This is a description of the study participants

claim: Each participant completed three experimental sessions and one to two sessions of retinotopic mapping and anatomical scans
source: Each participant completed three experimental sessions (two for the WM task and one for the control task, ~1 hr 30 min each) and one to two sessions of retinotopic mapping and anatomical scans (~2 hr).
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol

claim: Stimuli were created by multiplying a carrier grating with a modulator grating
source: Stimuli were created by multiplying two gratings (a carrier and a modulator; Figure 1C; Roth et al., 2018).
evidence: This describes the stimulus generation method

claim: The carrier grating consisted of a large, oriented sinusoidal Cartesian grating with contrast = 0.8 and spatial frequency = 1 cycle/°
source: The carrier grating consisted of a large, oriented sinusoidal Cartesian grating (contrast = 0.8, spatial frequency = 1 cycle/°) presented within an annulus (inner diameter: 1.2°; outer diameter: 12°).
evidence: This describes the stimulus parameters

claim: 180 orientations were generated for the carrier grating to cover the whole orientation space during the continuous report task
source: We generated 180 orientations for the carrier grating to cover the whole orientation space during the continuous report task.
evidence: This describes the stimulus design

claim: The modulator grating was polar-transformed and square wave with hard edges
source: The modulator grating was polar-transformed and square wave with hard edges, so that when multiplying with the carrier, it alternates the phase of the carrier and creates apertures.
evidence: This describes the modulator properties

claim: On half of the runs, the modulator produced a set of rings starting from the fovea (radial modulator)
source: On half of the runs, the modulator produced a set of rings starting from the fovea (radial modulator, scaled with eccentricity).
evidence: This describes the experimental design

claim: On the other half of the runs, the modulator produced a set of inward-pointing wedges encircling the fovea (angular modulator)
source: While on the other half of the runs, the modulator produced a set of inward-pointing wedges encircling the fovea (angular modulator).
evidence: This describes the experimental design

claim: The image-computable model of V1 predicted a radial preference for the radial modulated gratings
source: Importantly, the image-computable model of V1 (described below; Roth et al., 2018; Simoncelli et al., 1992) predicted a radial preference for the radial modulated gratings, but a tangential preference for the angular modulated gratings.
evidence: This describes model predictions

claim: The image-computable model of V1 predicted a tangential preference for the angular modulated gratings
source: Importantly, the image-computable model of V1 (described below; Roth et al., 2018; Simoncelli et al., 1992) predicted a radial preference for the radial modulated gratings, but a tangential preference for the angular modulated gratings.
evidence: This describes model predictions

claim: The radial modulator induced a bias that is consistent with the carrier orientation
source: Therefore, the radial modulator induced a bias that is consistent with the carrier orientation while the angular modulator induced a bias that is orthogonal to the carrier orientation.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the model predictions

claim: The angular modulator induced a bias that is orthogonal to the carrier orientation
source: Therefore, the radial modulator induced a bias that is consistent with the carrier orientation while the angular modulator induced a bias that is orthogonal to the carrier orientation.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the model predictions

claim: When changing the orientation of the stimuli for each trial, only the orientation of the carrier grating changed but not the modulator grating
source: Importantly, when changing the orientation of the stimuli for each trial, it only changed the orientation of the carrier grating but not the modulator grating.
evidence: This describes the experimental design

claim: Any fMRI activity measured could be attributed to either the orientation of the carrier grating, or an interaction between the orientation of the carrier grating and the static modulator grating
source: Therefore, any fMRI activity measured could be attributed to either the orientation of the carrier grating, or an interaction between the orientation of the carrier grating and the static modulator grating.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the experimental design

claim: Each participant completed two sessions for the WM task and one session for the control task on separate days
source: Each participant completed two sessions for the WM task and one session for the control task on separate days.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol

claim: Each WM session consisted of 10 runs with 12 trials per run
source: For both tasks, each session consisted of 10 runs, which cost 1.5–2 hr. Each run had 12 trials for the WM task and 24 trials for the control task.
evidence: This describes the experimental design

claim: Each control task session consisted of 10 runs with 24 trials per run
source: For both tasks, each session consisted of 10 runs, which cost 1.5–2 hr. Each run had 12 trials for the WM task and 24 trials for the control task.
evidence: This describes the experimental design

claim: Participants completed 240 trials in total for both tasks
source: Thus, participants completed 240 trials in total for both tasks.
evidence: This is calculated from the experimental design

claim: For each run, the target orientation were 15°, 75°, and 135° clockwise from vertical with random jitter (<7°)
source: For each run, the target orientation (i.e. the carrier's orientation) were 15°, 75°, and 135° clockwise from vertical with random jitter (<7°).
evidence: This describes the stimulus parameters

claim: In the WM task, participants maintained the oriented stimuli over a 12 s retention interval
source: For the WM task (left), participants maintained the oriented stimuli over a 12 s retention interval and rotated a recall probe to match their memory.
evidence: This describes the task procedure shown in Figure 1B

claim: In the WM task, participants rotated a recall probe to match their memory
source: For the WM task (left), participants maintained the oriented stimuli over a 12 s retention interval and rotated a recall probe to match their memory.
evidence: This describes the task procedure shown in Figure 1B

claim: In the perceptual control task, participants viewed the stimuli twice in a row with a short ISI and decided which one has a higher contrast
source: For the perceptual control task (right), participants viewed the stimuli twice in a row with a short ISI and asked to decide which one has a higher contrast; it places no demand on remembering orientation.
evidence: This describes the task procedure shown in Figure 1B

claim: The perceptual control task places no demand on remembering orientation
source: For the perceptual control task (right), participants viewed the stimuli twice in a row with a short ISI and asked to decide which one has a higher contrast; it places no demand on remembering orientation.
evidence: This is a characterization of the task design

claim: 97.72% (radial) and 96.79% (angular) of eye position sample points during the delay epoch were within 2° eccentricity from the center
source: Overall, 97.72% (radial) and 96.79% (angular) of the total number of eye position sample points during the delay epoch of the WM task across all subjects were within 2° eccentricity from the center (the fixation and the stimulus subtended 0.8° and 12° diameter, respectively).
evidence: This is data from eye-tracking analysis

claim: The circular correlation between the polar angle of the target orientation and the polar angle of the eye positions was not significant for both modulators
source: The circular correlation between the polar angle of the target orientation and the polar angle of the eye positions was not significant for both the radial (mean = 0.030, s.d.=0.103, t(14)=1.141, p=0.273) and the angular (mean = 0.001, s.d.=0.099, t(14)=0.056, p=0.956) modulator, suggesting that the eye movements could not account for our findings.
evidence: This is data from eye-tracking analysis with statistical tests

claim: Eye movements could not account for the findings
source: The circular correlation between the polar angle of the target orientation and the polar angle of the eye positions was not significant for both the radial (mean = 0.030, s.d.=0.103, t(14)=1.141, p=0.273) and the angular (mean = 0.001, s.d.=0.099, t(14)=0.056, p=0.956) modulator, suggesting that the eye movements could not account for our findings.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the eye-tracking analysis
